entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17669"/><div sID="gen35699" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17669"/><hi type="bold">3. once named--</hi>Greek, "Let it not be even named" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.4">Ep 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.12">12</reference>). "Uncleanness" and "covetousness" are taken up again from <reference osisRef="Eph.4.19">Ep 4:19</reference>. The two are so closely allied that the Greek for "covetousness" (pleonexia) is used sometimes in Scripture, and often in the Greek Fathers, for sins of impurity. The common principle is the longing to fill one's desire with material objects of sense, outside of God. The expression, "not be even named," applies better to impurity, than to "covetousness." <div eID="gen35699" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17682"/><div sID="gen35732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17682"/><hi type="bold">16. Redeeming the time--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Col.4.5">Col 4:5</reference>). Greek, "Buying up for yourselves the seasonable time" (whenever it occurs) of good to yourselves and to others. Buying off from the vanities of "them that are without" (<reference osisRef="Col.4.5">Col 4:5</reference>), and of the "unwise" (here in Ephesians), the opportune time afforded to you for the work of God. In a narrower sense, special favorable seasons for good, occasionally presenting themselves, are referred to, of which believers ought diligently to avail themselves. This constitutes true "wisdom" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.15">Ep 5:15</reference>). In a larger sense, the whole season from the time that one is spiritually awakened, is to be "redeemed" from vanity for God (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.2">2Co 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.2-1Pet.4.4">1Pe 4:2-4</reference>). "Redeem" implies the preciousness of the opportune season, a jewel to be bought at any price. Wahl explains, "Redeeming for yourselves (that is, availing yourselves of) the opportunity (offered you of acting aright), and commanding the time as a master does his servant." Tittmann, "Watch the time, and make it your own so as to control it; as merchants look out for opportunities, and accurately choose out the best goods; serve not the time, but command it, and it shall do what you approve." So Pindar [Pythia, 4.509], "The time followed him as his servant, and was not as a runaway slave."<div eID="gen35732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because the days are evil--</hi>The days of life in general are so exposed to evil, as to make it necessary to make the most of the seasonable opportunity so long as it lasts (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.13">Ep 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.47.9">Ge 47:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.5">Psa 49:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Ec 11:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.1">12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.35">Joh 12:35</reference>). Besides, there are many special evil days (in persecution, sickness, &c.) when the Christian is laid by in silence; therefore he needs the more to improve the seasonable times afforded to him (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Am 5:13</reference>), which Paul perhaps alludes to. <div eID="gen35733" type="x-p"/>

As, therefore, He brought to His feet one that so treated Him, and that even wantonly spurned Him, by much tenderness of regard, not by threats, insults, and terror: so also do you act towards your wife, and though you see her disdainful and wantonly wayward, you will be able to bring her to your feet by much thoughtfulness for her, by love, by kindness. For no bound is more sovereign in binding than such bonds, especially in the case of husband and wife. For one may constrain a servant by fear, though not even he is so to be bound to you; for he may readily run away. But the companion of your life, the mother of your children, the basis of all your joy, you ought to bind to you, not by fear and threats, but by love and attachment" [Chrysostom]. gave himself-- Greek, "gave Himself up." for it-- Translate, "for her." The relation of the Church to Christ is the ground of Christianity's having raised woman to her due place in the social scale, from which she was, and is, excluded in heathen lands.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17693"/><div sID="gen35769" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17693"/><hi type="bold">27. he--</hi>The oldest manuscripts and authorities read, "That He might Himself present unto Himself the Church glorious," namely, as a bride (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2Co 11:2</reference>). Holiness and glory are inseparable. "Cleansing" is the necessary preliminary to both. Holiness is glory internal; glory is holiness shining forth outwardly. The laver of baptism is the vehicle, but the word is the nobler and true instrument of the cleansing [Bengel]. It is Christ that prepares the Church with the necessary ornaments of grace, for presentation to Himself, as the Bridegroom at His coming again (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.1">Mt 25:1</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">Re 19:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">21:2</reference>).<div eID="gen35769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not having spot--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Song.4.7">So 4:7</reference>). The visible Church now contains clean and unclean together, like Noah's ark; like the wedding room which contained some that had, and others that had not, the wedding garment (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.10-Matt.22.14">Mt 22:10-14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.20">2Ti 2:20</reference>); or as the good and bad fish are taken in the same net because it cannot discern the bad from the good, the fishermen being unable to know what kind of fish the nets have taken under the waves. Still the Church is termed "holy" in the creed, in reference to her ideal and ultimate destination. When the Bridegroom comes, the bride shall be presented to Him wholly without spot, the evil being cut off from the body for ever (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.47-Matt.13.50">Mt 13:47-50</reference>). Not that there are two churches, one with bad and good intermingled, another in which there are good alone; but one and the same Church in relation to different times, now with good and evil together, hereafter with good alone [Pearson]. <div eID="gen35770" type="x-p"/>

For--</hi>Greek, "Because" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.15">1Co 6:15</reference>). Christ nourisheth and cherisheth the Church as being of one flesh with Him. Translate, "Because we are members of His body (His literal body), being OF His flesh and of His bones" [Alford] (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.23">Ge 2:23</reference>, 24). The Greek expresses, "Being formed out of" or "of the substance of His flesh." Adam's deep sleep, wherein Eve was formed from out of his opened side, is an emblem of Christ's death, which was the birth of the Spouse, the Church. <reference osisRef="John.12.24">Joh 12:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.19.34">19:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.19.35">35</reference>, to which <reference osisRef="Eph.5.25-Eph.5.27">Ep 5:25-27</reference> allude, as implying atonement by His blood, and sanctification by the "water," answering to that which flowed from His side (compare also <reference osisRef="John.7.38">Joh 7:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.7.39">39</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1Co 6:11</reference>). As Adam gave Eve a new name, Hebrew, "Isha," "woman," formed from his own rib, Ish, "man," signifying her formation from him, so Christ, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.17">Re 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.12">3:12</reference>. <reference osisRef="Gen.2.21">Ge 2:21</reference>, 23, 24 puts the bones first because the reference there is to the natural structure. But Paul is referring to the flesh of Christ. It is not our bones and flesh, but "we" that are spiritually propagated (in our soul and spirit now, and in the body hereafter, regenerated) from the manhood of Christ which has flesh and bones. We are members of His glorified body (<reference osisRef="John.6.53">Joh 6:53</reference>). The two oldest existing manuscripts, and Coptic or Memphitic version, omit "of His flesh and of His bones"; the words may have crept into the text through the Margin from <reference osisRef="Gen.2.23">Ge 2:23</reference>, Septuagint. However, Irenæus, 294, and the old Latin and Vulgate versions, with some good old manuscripts, have them. <div eID="gen35778" type="x-p"/>

For--</hi>The propagation of the Church from Christ, as that of Eve from Adam, is the foundation of the spiritual marriage. The natural marriage, wherein "a man leaves father and mother (the oldest manuscripts omit 'his') and is joined unto his wife," is not the principal thing meant here, but the spiritual marriage represented by it, and on which it rests, whereby Christ left the Father's bosom to woo to Himself the Church out of a lost world: <reference osisRef="Eph.5.32">Ep 5:32</reference> proves this: His earthly mother as such, also, He holds in secondary account as compared with His spiritual Bride (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.48">Lu 2:48</reference>, 49; <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.19-2Cor.8.21">8:19-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.27">11:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.28">28</reference>). He shall again leave His Father's abode to consummate the union (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.1-Matt.25.10">Mt 25:1-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">Re 19:7</reference>).<div eID="gen35779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they two shall be one flesh--</hi>So the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, &c., read (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.24">Ge 2:24</reference>), instead of "they shall be one flesh." So <reference osisRef="Matt.19.5">Mt 19:5</reference>. In natural marriage, husband and wife combine the elements of one perfect human being: the one being incomplete without the other. So Christ, as God-man, is pleased to make the Church, the body, a necessary adjunct to Himself, the Head. He is the archetype of the Church, from whom and according to whom, as the pattern, she is formed. He is her Head, as the husband is of the wife (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.5">Ro 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.3">1Co 11:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.45">15:45</reference>). Christ will never allow any power to sever Himself and His bride, indissolubly joined (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.6">Mt 19:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.28">Joh 10:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.10.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.13.1">13:1</reference>). <div eID="gen35780" type="x-p"/>

Rather, "This mystery is a great one." This profound truth, beyond man's power of discovering, but now revealed, namely, of the spiritual union of Christ and the Church, represented by the marriage union, is a great one, of deep import.
